papers.title: Ear Reconstruction in Young Children
papers.abstract: The use of a porous high-density polyethylene ear implant, rather than a costal cartilage framework, allows ear reconstruction in young children before they enter school. The fact that the growth of the normal ear matures early allows for good symmetry. If the implant is covered completely with a large, well-vascularized superficial parietal fascia flap and appropriately color-matched skin, an ear with excellent projection and definition can be obtained with minimal complications and long-term viability. Ear reconstruction in young children is preferred by the author because the necessary fascial flap coverage is thinner, easier to harvest than in older patients, and can be done in a single outpatient procedure with minimal discomfort or psychological trauma.

papers.title: Complications after Total Porous Implant Ear Reconstruction and Their Management
papers.abstract: Microtia reconstruction using porous polyethylene implants has become an established alternative to autologous costal cartilage techniques. Few surgeons are trained in porous implant ear reconstruction (PIER), leading to a relative lack of understanding of the nuances of this type of surgery. The risks of exposure, infection, and fracture of the implant have further discouraged surgeons from performing PIERs. Meticulous technique and proper management of complications are critical to the success of surgeries involving porous implants (Medpor, Su-Por). There are a limited number of articles in the literature that report the management of complications of porous implant auricular reconstruction. The purpose of this work is to present a comprehensive review of the management of complications with PIER based on over 10 years of experience with this surgical technique.

papers.title: Porous Polyethylene Implant and Rib Cartilage in Ear Reconstruction: A Comparison
papers.abstract: Auricular reconstruction, known as the "surgical art," is one of the most difficult and complex surgeries in medicine. There are two different techniques that involve either the use of artificial material like porous polyethylene (PE) or the patient's own rib cartilage graft. The patient's indication, age, conditions requiring previous failed surgeries, and the surgeon's skill in creating the frame are the most important factors in the choice of technique. Both methods are performed in our clinic in Vienna. We experienced more complications in the early cases using PE due to surgical inexperience. The advantages of PE, such as the fact that it is a single-stage surgery, favorable aesthetic appearance (definition and projection), and the possibility of combining the reconstruction with bone conduction devices or active middle ear implants and performing in older patients, can be compared with its disadvantages, such as greater complications. Both techniques require the acquisition of considerable skill and tricks, and for this reason it is important that a skilled surgeon who has mastered these auricular reconstruction skills is available to teach the next generation.

papers.title: A Simple Up-Scalable Thermal Treatment Method for Synthesis of ZnO Nanoparticles
papers.abstract: A simple thermal treatment method, utilizing only zinc nitrate, polyvinyl pyrrolidone (PVP), and deionized water, was used to synthesize ZnO nanoparticles, and their characteristics were investigated by various techniques. The TGA measurement demonstrated that the bulk of the capping agent PVP can be removed at temperatures higher than 500 °C and is consistent with the absence of the majority of PVP absorption peaks in the FT-IR spectra. The formation of almost pure ZnO nanoparticles was established by the presence of single absorption peak in the FT-IR spectra due to being only Zn–O bonds at calcination temperatures of 500 °C and above. The TEM images revealed that the nanoparticles have a spherical shape and the particle size increased from 60.1–83.1 nm with an increase in calcination temperatures from 500–600 °C. The XRD diffraction patterns indicated that the particles are of a wurzite lattice structure. The optical properties were determined by UV-Vis spectrophotometer, and it was found that the band gap of ZnO nanoparticles decreased from 3.249–3.239 eV with an increase in calcination temperature from 500–600 °C.

papers.title: Great Teaching‐Observe It, Emulate It, and Pass it On!
papers.abstract: Dr. Gabriel Keith Harris Nicewander, Menking, Wiliston, Parkes, Hibschman, and Rice. These are the last names of just a few of the teachers that inspired me as I made my way through elementary, middle, and high school, and into community college. The topics they taught varied, but two things were constant – a great depth of knowledge and great enthusiasm in communicating it. My Marine Corps drill instructors had the same teaching qualities (although they tended to deliver their lessons at a very high volume). By the time I began to work on a Master's degree in Food Science, I had started to pay attention not just to the course topics, but also the way in which they were taught. Professors like Dr. David Dickey, Dr. Lynn Turner, Dr. Bernadene Magnuson, Dr. Grady Chism, and the late Dr. David Min gave me great examples to follow. I am forever grateful to Dr. Min for allowing me to help teach a Food Analysis lab for two semesters in a row. That experience settled it once and for all. I wanted to be a teacher! Now, when I consider the past Cruess Award winners I have had the honor to know and work with, I am humbled to be included among them. For that reason, I am grateful that these outstanding role models cared enough to invest their time and effort in me as a student. Finally, I am indebted to the students who serve as a continual inspiration to be a better teacher. Thanks to all of you! Science is boring. Science is hard. Well, yes, it can be. Science taught in the abstract, an isolated equation or a long list of facts, is boring to most everyone (including me). Let's admit it, some scientific concepts can be very difficult to grasp at first. Why not tell students about the exciting applications of science first in order to generate a “need to know”? Applied science allows us to fly airplanes, print in 3-D, and provides for near-instantaneous worldwide communication. It allows us to produce the food that feeds the world. Now, that's exciting. That's fun! What field is more applied than Food Science? (It's science you can eat, after all.) I see food and the science of food as an easily accessible gateway for understanding both basic and applied sciences - physics, chemistry, engineering, microbiology, mathematics, psychology, and many others. Why? Because it applies directly to me (and to you). What is more relatable than food? After all, most of us are fortunate enough to “relate” to food three or more times per day. Food is a great way to interest students in science. My teaching philosophy, in a nutshell, is that I have two roles to play, both inside and outside of the classroom: personal trainer and storyteller. Much like a personal trainer in a gym, I cannot do the hard work required to master a topic for students. Students must do the intense mental “exercises” for themselves. They must practice their skills regularly. What I can do is recognize talent, encourage hard work, and provide motivation and support. I can work to provide an atmosphere (a mental gymnasium of sorts) that is conducive to learning. I can challenge students to push harder and go farther than they thought possible. At the end of the day, however, they must do the hard work themselves. That is why I believe so strongly in active learning. Students who “get their hands dirty” in the laboratory, who are actively writing, who are discussing problem sets, or who are finding solutions to real problems won't have to memorize lists of facts. What they learn will become a part of them, an ingrained skill like catching a baseball or riding a bike. As a storyteller, I feel that my job is to help link what students already know to what they need to know. One way to do this is to tell vivid stories that spark student interest in a particular topic. I remember watching a student enter my introductory food science course every day with an angry look on his face. Arms folded and looking off into nowhere, it was obvious that he did not want to be there. But, when the lecture topic switched from food chemistry to food law (generally not the most exciting topic for students), his demeanor changed completely. His arms unfolded. He leaned forward. He asked questions. It turned out that he was a political science major with aspirations to become an attorney. He had no idea that food law existed until that moment. When students see that a topic relates to them personally, something that was once boring and difficult becomes exciting and challenging. For this reason, I think that it is essential to understand that each class we teach is different every semester we teach it. We need to tell the right story at the right time to the right audience to be most effective as teachers. Like all things, teaching is temporary. The fact that every lecture brings me closer to the last lecture I will ever deliver means that there is a certain urgency in the sharing of my knowledge. It makes me want to give my best effort each and every time I step into the lab or the classroom. It makes me want to continually improve as a teacher. Many of the teachers that I have so admired over the years have moved into retirement or are no longer with us. I view the knowledge they have imparted as a baton that they have passed on to me. With the support of family, friends, and colleagues, I will do my best to run my part of the relay and train the next generation of scholars. What a great honor and blessing it is to have this precious opportunity to teach students, if only for a short time!
